21	- Year / venue: 2026, arXiv (preprint, not peer-reviewed; v1 dated 16 Sep 2026). Affiliations: KAIST, Microsoft Research Montréal, Microsoft AI (p. 1).
22	- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2609.18805 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18805
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
24	
25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
27	
28	## 1. Research objective
29	- [A] Evaluate coding agents on "reference-guided" software engineering: inferring intended behaviour by interacting with a working web application, then implementing it in an incomplete or empty application. This differs from benchmarks where behaviour is given as an issue or instruction (p. 1).
30	- [A] Turn working interactive web apps into a scalable, automatically built source of verifiable tasks ("application-to-task factorization") with controllable difficulty ("restoration depth") (p. 2).
31	
32	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
33	- Not stated as formal RQs. [A] Guiding question: "Can we uncover this latent behavioral structure and use it to turn a working interactive web application into a scalable source of verifiable software-engineering tasks?" (p. 2). [I] Implicit empirical questions: how well agents restore masked features and rebuild whole apps from a live reference, how performance changes with the number of dependent behaviours, and why agents fail.
34	
35	## 3. Methodology
36	- Research design: [V] A fully automated LLM pipeline ("mine–craft–patch") builds tasks; two evaluation settings follow, plus trajectory and failure analyses (p. 2; p. 6).
37	- Approach / model / intervention:
38	  - [V] *Mine*: LLM agents (Planner, Collector, Relabeler, Reflector), with read access to the source and the live app, propose behaviour goals, drive the app through a Playwright browser helper, and record replayable traces of actions plus expected observable signals (accessible names, visible text, URL, state). A trace is admitted only if it replays deterministically from a reset state (p. 3; p. 4; p. 25).
39	  - [V] *Craft*: an LLM masks (deletes) the source implementing a behaviour, either logic only or logic plus UI. A mask is accepted only if the app still builds, prerequisite traces still pass, the target trace fails, and an LLM "mask-depth critic" judges the deletion substantive. Masks along a prerequisite lineage are combined into cumulative tasks, and the reversed mask is the gold patch, which must replay the whole lineage (p. 4; p. 5; p. 6).
40	  - [V] *Patch*, partial-application reconstruction: the agent gets the masked repository, an LLM-written behavioural problem statement, and browser access to the live reference (no reference source, no internet) (p. 6).
41	  - [V] *Patch*, full-application reconstruction: the agent starts from a minimal scaffold plus a product-level capability description and must rebuild the whole app from the live reference (p. 6; p. 10; p. 11).
42	  - [V] All construction stages use GPT-5.6 Sol (p. 2; p. 7).
43	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] 9 frontier models compared on partial reconstruction; 3 models (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol) on full reconstruction. Logic-only vs logic-and-UI masks; restoration depths 1–8 (p. 8; p. 11). No human or non-agent baseline.
44	- [I] Relation to our topic: full-application reconstruction is very close to our scenario of rebuilding a web application by observing its UI and behaviour, with no access to its source. Partial reconstruction resembles restoring missing features in an existing codebase by consulting a working product.
45	
46	## 4. Dataset and sample
47	- Data source(s): [V] 26 self-contained web apps: 18 adapted from the OSWorld web-application suite and 8 real-world open-source projects or SaaS clones (Actual Budget, Reactive Resume, Baserow, two Trello clones, two Jira clones, a Calendly clone), using Django, Angular, React and Next.js with SQL and document back ends. Each is pinned to a commit (p. 19).
48	- Sample size (N) and unit:
49	  - [V] Mining: 2,800 candidate goals, 2,350 collected, 2,165 reproduced and 1,975 verified behaviours; maximum lineage depth 17 (mean 3.40) (p. 7).
50	  - [V] Tasks: 4,063 in total, 2,862 atomic and 1,201 cumulative; 1,997 logic-only and 2,066 logic-and-UI (p. 7).
51	  - [V] Per-app task counts are very uneven, from 2 (ExpenseFlow) to 372 (Reactive Resume) (p. 19).
52	  - [V] Evaluation suite ProgramDistill-300: 50 atomic and 250 cumulative tasks covering 269 lineages and all 26 apps (p. 8).
53	  - [V] Full reconstruction: 12 apps, 590 atomic and 413 cumulative behaviour tests, 36 runs (p. 11; p. 12).
54	- Sampling / selection method: [V] ProgramDistill-300 is stratified by restoration depth (quotas 50, 45, 45, 40, 35, 30, 30, 25 for depths 1–8) and selected round-robin across apps (p. 8). [I] Why these 26 apps, and why these 12 for full reconstruction ("twelve stateful web applications", p. 11), is not explained beyond "complementary sources" (p. 3).
55	- Data availability (public? link?): [A] "We are working on a public release of the ProgramDistill benchmark" (p. 1). Not yet released at time of writing; prompts are given in the appendix (p. 25; p. 30; p. 33).
56	
57	## 5. Experimental setup
58	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Modified R2E-Gym harness with tools `execute_bash`, `file_editor`, `search` and `finish`. A browser CLI drives both the reference and the current app (p. 8). Agents see only structured text observations (visible text, element IDs, roles, accessible names, input values); full reconstruction additionally exposes selectors. Screenshots and raw HTML are excluded (p. 3; p. 24).
59	- [V] Partial reconstruction: reasoning effort high, at most 1,000 steps, 150k-token history cutoff. Full reconstruction: reasoning effort max, at most 10,000 steps, 500k-token cutoff. Per-tool timeout 90 s, no aggregate time limit (p. 24).
60	- [V] Determinism: application state is reset before each collection and replay, and a shared fake clock (libfaketime plus a browser Date offset) is used (p. 3; p. 19; p. 20).
61	- [V] Isolation: the reference is reachable only via the browser helper, public egress is blocked, there is no pre-mask git history, and grading traces are private. Submissions are rebuilt and replayed in a fresh verifier (p. 10; p. 23; p. 24).
62	- [V] The full-reconstruction scaffold requires an `app.js` exporting `async function handle(req, res, context)`, with state kept in `context.state` (p. 37).
63	- [V] Number of runs: one per model and task (partial) and one per model and app (36 full-reconstruction runs, p. 12). Repeats or seeds: not reported.
64	- [V] Cost: tokens x LiteLLM list prices (p. 37). One GPT-6 Astra pass over 300 tasks took about 557 minutes on 4 servers (p. 37).
65	- Code availability: [A] release in progress (p. 1).
66	
67	## 6. Evaluation metrics
68	- Replay verifier V(A, L): returns 1 only if every recorded browser action completes and every expected signal is satisfied, replaying the whole prerequisite lineage without LLM involvement (p. 4).
69	- Binary score: 1 only if the complete lineage passes after the agent's patch. Chain score: fraction of repair targets passed, giving partial credit (p. 6).
70	- Full reconstruction: atomic behaviour recovery (fraction of single-behaviour tests passed, with prerequisites replayed) and cumulative workflow recovery (binary and chain) (p. 6; p. 11).
71	- [V] Source-level matching is not required: function names, variables and structure may differ if behaviour replays (p. 6). [V] In full reconstruction, however, selectors and accessible names must match the reference, because evaluation "replays user interactions using selectors" (p. 35).
72	- Diagnostics: interaction counts (observation, read/search, edit/write steps), share of unchanged target files and retained stub lines, shortcut-attempt rate, failure categories (p. 9; p. 10; p. 12).
73	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [V] None; means only. Pearson correlations between prompt size and binary score are reported in the context-length check (p. 40).
74	
75	## 7. Key findings
76	1. [V] Partial reconstruction (ProgramDistill-300): mean binary score is 84.3% for GPT-6 Astra, 68.7% for Claude Opus 5 and 60.7% for GPT-5.6 Sol, with a middle tier at 45.3–48.3% and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview lowest at 22.3%. Mean cost per trajectory is $33.99, $28.86 and $16.01 for the top three (p. 8; p. 38).
77	2. [V] Success drops with restoration depth: Astra falls from 100% at depth 1 to 64.0% at depth 8, Opus 5 from 96% to 32.0% and Sol from 92% to 32.0%; every other model keeps less than half of its depth-1 performance (p. 8; p. 9).
78	3. [V] Restoring UI as well as logic is harder. Binary scores for logic-only vs logic-and-UI masks are 92.9% vs 76.9% for Astra and 76.4% vs 46.9% for Sol (p. 38).
79	4. [V] Full-application reconstruction (12 apps): Astra recovers 58.98% of atomic behaviours and 49.15% of cumulative workflows, Opus 5 42.03% and 28.81%, and Sol 33.39% and 21.07% (p. 11). Per-app results vary widely, e.g. Astra's cumulative recovery ranges from 81.8% (MailHub) to 5.9% (Baserow) (p. 11).
80	5. [V] Of 977 failed atomic behaviours in full reconstruction, 59.2% were never observed in the reference. Of the rest, 1.8% were observed but not implemented, 11.1% were implemented with the wrong observable form and 27.9% produced the wrong state, route or result (p. 12).
81	6. [A] Agents' own validation (syntax checks, successful requests, selected text matches) often did not recheck the failing workflow after the last relevant edit, so mismatches went undetected (p. 12; p. 13).
82	7. [V] From depth 1 to 8, code to restore grows 9.3x and required browser actions 10.7x, but reference-observation steps per target fall from 34.60 to 8.46. Retained mask stub lines rise from 11.1% to 24.6% (p. 9; p. 10).
83	8. [V] The depth effect persists among runs with similar context lengths; e.g. in the 40–80k band, mean binary score falls from 82.6% at depth 1 to 24.2% at depth 8 (p. 39).
84	9. [V] At least one shortcut attempt (git history, public source fetch, harness probing, direct reference access) appears in 7.2% of trajectories: 19.0% for Grok 4.6, 17.7% for Gemini 3.1 Pro and 0.3% for Astra. These channels were blocked by design (p. 10).
85	10. [V] The best model was the most observation-heavy and edit-light: Astra averages 96.3 current-app observation steps and 9.9 edit/write steps per trajectory (p. 9).
86	
87	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
88	- [A] Agents receive structured text observations, not screenshots. Visual fidelity is not evaluated and "would require criteria beyond the current replay-based behavioral checks" (p. 14).
89	- [A] Only self-contained web apps; external services, nondeterministic state, and desktop/mobile apps are future work (p. 14).
90	- [A] Benchmark coverage and quality depend on the construction model (GPT-5.6 Sol) (p. 15).
91	- [A] Results depend on the browser/agent infrastructure (replay-stable selectors, settled observations, harness), and sensitivity to these choices is uncharacterised (p. 15).
92	- [A] The isolation is not a general-purpose sandbox for hostile code (p. 24).
93	- [A] Possible misuse for cloning proprietary apps; experiments are limited to public/open-source apps (p. 15).
94	
95	## 9. Limitations we identified
96	- [I] Code quality and maintainability of the rebuilt or repaired code are not measured at all. Only behavioural replay is scored (p. 6). The full-reconstruction contract forces a single Node `handle()` entry with in-memory `context.state` (p. 37), while the originals use Django, Angular, React or Next.js with databases (p. 19). The rebuild's architecture is therefore imposed and not comparable to the original.
97	- [I] Possible self-preference and family bias:
98	  - GPT-5.6 Sol builds the traces, masks and problem statements (p. 2) and is also an evaluated model; the top model is from the same vendor (GPT-6 Astra) (p. 8).
99	  - The full-reconstruction failure analysis is done by GPT-6 Astra (p. 12), which judges its own and its competitors' failures, with no human validation reported.
100	- [I] No human check anywhere. Tasks are built "without human intervention" (p. 1), mask depth is judged by an LLM critic (p. 5), and 572 cumulative masks were merged by an LLM agent (p. 6). The only quality evidence is the replay checks and the 100% depth-1 solve rate of one model (p. 8). No sample of tasks was manually audited.
101	- [I] Oracle completeness is not measured. Unlike ProgramBench, no code coverage is reported for the trace suites. Behaviours exist only if the mining LLM found and stably replayed them; 29.5% of goals were lost (p. 7). Behaviours an agent never observes still count as failures (59.2% of failures, p. 12), but the trace bank itself may miss large parts of each app.
102	- [I] The full-reconstruction oracle checks surface identity (selectors, accessible names, labels) (p. 35), and the agent is shown the reference's selectors (p. 24). This mixes functional fidelity with DOM-level mimicry. A functionally equivalent rebuild with different labels would fail, while visual appearance is not checked at all (p. 14).
103	- [I] Contamination is not discussed. The 8 real-world apps are public GitHub projects (p. 19), so agents may partly reconstruct masked code from memory, especially for well-known clones.
104	- [I] Small and uneven samples for headline claims: one run per cell, full reconstruction on 12 apps x 3 models (36 runs) (p. 12), and per-app task pools from 2 to 372 (p. 19). Differences between close models (e.g. 45.3% vs 45.7%, p. 8) are not interpretable without variance estimates.
105	- [I] The model names (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol) were very recent at publication and are cited to system cards (p. 16; p. 17). Results may not be reproducible once these API versions change.
106	
107	## 10. Threats to validity
108	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [V] Leakage controls: no pre-mask git history, blocked egress, hidden grading files, browser-only reference access, fresh-verifier rebuild (p. 10; p. 24). [I] Remaining threats: the same model family builds and is evaluated; LLM-only task validation; memorisation of public source.
109	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] 26 mostly small, self-contained CRUD-style web apps, 18 of them from one synthetic suite (OSWorld) (p. 19); a single harness; text-only observation (p. 14). Transfer to large production apps, visual-design fidelity or human-in-the-loop vibe coding is untested.
110	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] Replay of mined traces is a sound behavioural oracle for the traced workflows, but it covers only discovered behaviours and also demands selector-level identity (p. 35). "Reconstruction success" therefore means reproducing specific recorded interactions, not the whole application.
111	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No CIs or tests; single runs; stratified 300-task subset. The depth trend is consistent across models and context bands (p. 39), which makes that particular finding more credible.
112	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Prompts, harness settings and pricing are reported in detail (p. 24; p. 25; p. 37). [A] The benchmark is not yet public (p. 1).
113	
114	## 11. Future research directions
115	- Stated by authors [A] (p. 14; p. 15):
116	  - add screenshots and visual-fidelity criteria;
117	  - extend to external services, nondeterministic state, and desktop and mobile apps;
118	  - study the quality–cost trade-off of the construction model;
119	  - characterise sensitivity to infrastructure choices;
120	  - use the tasks and trajectories for training (distillation, RL, curriculum by restoration depth).
121	- Suggested by us [I]:
122	  1. Measure code quality and maintainability of rebuilt apps, with a free architecture rather than a single fixed handler.
123	  2. Audit a sample of mined traces and masks by hand, and measure oracle coverage.
124	  3. Use a construction model from a different family than the evaluated models.
125	  4. Add repeated runs.
126	  5. Study a human-in-the-loop (vibe-coding) condition in which a developer steers reconstruction.
127	
128	## 12. Relevance to our research
129	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ4, RQ5 (RQ3 only as a documented gap).
130	- How it informs our work [I]: This is the closest available study of rebuilding *interactive web applications* from a running reference via its UI, which is our core scenario. It offers a reusable fidelity-testing method: deterministic replay of recorded browser workflows with expected signals and prerequisite lineages. It also gives a failure taxonomy showing that most misses come from not exploring the reference rather than from coding errors (p. 12). It shows that agents' self-validation is unreliable (p. 12). Together with ProgramBench (yang2026programbench), it shows that functional fidelity of whole-app rebuilds remains far from complete. Like ProgramBench, it does not measure the maintainability of the rebuilt code, which supports the joint fidelity-plus-quality gap in RQ5.
131	
132	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
133	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
134	|---|---|---|---|---|
135	| RQ1 | Reference-guided setting: agent interacts with a live reference web app via a browser CLI (structured text observations, no source, no screenshots) and edits a masked repo or a blank scaffold to reproduce its behaviour. | p. 3; p. 6; p. 24 | V | moderate (design fact) |
136	| RQ2 | Best full-application rebuild from a live reference recovers 58.98% of atomic behaviours and 49.15% of cumulative workflows (12 apps); other models 21–42%. | p. 11 | V | weak (preprint, 36 single runs) |
137	| RQ2 | Partial-repair success falls as more dependent behaviours must be restored (best model 100% at depth 1 to 64% at depth 8; others to ≤32%), and the drop persists when context length is controlled. | p. 8; p. 9; p. 39 | V | weak (single runs, but consistent across 9 models) |
138	| RQ2 | Restoring UI plus logic is harder than logic alone (e.g. 92.9% vs 76.9% binary for the best model). | p. 38 | V | weak |
139	| RQ2 | 59.2% of failed behaviours in full rebuilds were never observed in the reference; 27.9% had wrong state/result and 11.1% wrong observable form. | p. 12 | V | weak (classified by an LLM that is also an evaluated model) |
140	| RQ4 | Fidelity oracle: deterministic browser-trace replay with expected signals, admitted only if replayable on the intact app, failing after masking, and passing with the gold patch. | p. 4; p. 5; p. 6 | V | moderate (design fact) |
141	| RQ4 | Agents' own validation (syntax checks, request success, partial text checks) missed behavioural mismatches with the reference. | p. 12 | A | weak |
142	| RQ4 | Tasks are built and validated without human intervention by one LLM (GPT-5.6 Sol), which is also evaluated; authors note quality depends on the construction model. | p. 1; p. 2; p. 15 | A | weak |
143	| RQ5 | Visual fidelity and screenshot-based observation are not evaluated; authors name them, plus desktop/mobile apps, as future work. Code quality of rebuilds is not measured (our observation). | p. 14 | A | weak |
144	
145	## 14. Key quotes
146	> "The distinction is thus a shift from specification consumption to specification discovery." (p. 14)
147	
148	> "the largest failure category is behavior that was not observed in the reference, accounting for 59.2% of failures" (p. 12)
149	
150	> "Similar text or element structure in observations is not sufficient." (p. 35)
151	
152	## Analyst notes
153	- Reading coverage: whole paper read, pp. 1–40, including all appendices and prompts. Figures 1, 6, 8–13 are partly garbled in the text layer, so only numbers stated in the text or tables are used. Figure 11 per-model shortcut rates were cross-checked with the text (p. 10).
154	- Uncertainties:
155	  - how the 26 and 12 apps were chosen;
156	  - whether trace suites cover most app functionality;
157	  - how much memorisation of public app source contributes.
158	  
159	  The future-dated model names (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5, Gemini 3.7 Flash) are taken as reported; the paper is dated 16 Sep 2026, before our analysis date.
160	- Strength ratings follow research-standards §5 (preprint without replication = weak). The depth-degradation finding is the most robust internally, because it is consistent across 9 models and context bands.
161

[A] Guiding question: "Can we uncover this latent behavioral structure and use it to turn a working interactive web application into a scalable source of verifiable software-engineering tasks?" (p. 2). 36	- Research design: [V] A fully automated LLM pipeline ("mine–craft–patch") builds tasks; two evaluation settings follow, plus trajectory and failure analyses (p. 2; p. 6).
37	- Approach / model / intervention:
38	  - [V] *Mine*: LLM agents (Planner, Collector, Relabeler, Reflector), with read access to the source and the live app, propose behaviour goals, drive the app through a Playwright browser helper, and record replayable traces of actions plus expected observable signals (accessible names, visible text, URL, state). A trace is admitted only if it replays deterministically from a reset state (p. 3; p. 4; p. 25).
39	  - [V] *Craft*: an LLM masks (deletes) the source implementing a behaviour, either logic only or logic plus UI. A mask is accepted only if the app still builds, prerequisite traces still pass, the target trace fails, and an LLM "mask-depth critic" judges the deletion substantive. Masks along a prerequisite lineage are combined into cumulative tasks, and the reversed mask is the gold patch, which must replay the whole lineage (p. 4; p. 5; p. 6).
40	  - [V] *Patch*, partial-application reconstruction: the agent gets the masked repository, an LLM-written behavioural problem statement, and browser access to the live reference (no reference source, no internet) (p. 6).
41	  - [V] *Patch*, full-application reconstruction: the agent starts from a minimal scaffold plus a product-level capability description and must rebuild the whole app from the live reference (p. 6; p. 10; p. 11).
42	  - [V] All construction stages use GPT-5.6 Sol (p. 2; p. 7).
43	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] 9 frontier models compared on partial reconstruction; 3 models (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol) on full reconstruction. Logic-only vs logic-and-UI masks; restoration depths 1–8 (p. 8; p. 11). No human or non-agent baseline.
44	- [I] Relation to our topic: full-application reconstruction is very close to our scenario of rebuilding a web application by observing its UI and behaviour, with no access to its source. Partial reconstruction resembles restoring missing features in an existing codebase by consulting a working product.
45	
46	## 4. Dataset and sample
47	- Data source(s): [V] 26 self-contained web apps: 18 adapted from the OSWorld web-application suite and 8 real-world open-source projects or SaaS clones (Actual Budget, Reactive Resume, Baserow, two Trello clones, two Jira clones, a Calendly clone), using Django, Angular, React and Next.js with SQL and document back ends. Each is pinned to a commit (p. 19).
48	- Sample size (N) and unit:
49	  - [V] Mining: 2,800 candidate goals, 2,350 collected, 2,165 reproduced and 1,975 verified behaviours; maximum lineage depth 17 (mean 3.40) (p. 7).
50	  - [V] Tasks: 4,063 in total, 2,862 atomic and 1,201 cumulative; 1,997 logic-only and 2,066 logic-and-UI (p. 7).
51	  - [V] Per-app task counts are very uneven, from 2 (ExpenseFlow) to 372 (Reactive Resume) (p. 19).
52	  - [V] Evaluation suite ProgramDistill-300: 50 atomic and 250 cumulative tasks covering 269 lineages and all 26 apps (p. 8).
53	  - [V] Full reconstruction: 12 apps, 590 atomic and 413 cumulative behaviour tests, 36 runs (p. 11; p. 12).
54	- Sampling / selection method: [V] ProgramDistill-300 is stratified by restoration depth (quotas 50, 45, 45, 40, 35, 30, 30, 25 for depths 1–8) and selected round-robin across apps (p. 8). [I] Why these 26 apps, and why these 12 for full reconstruction ("twelve stateful web applications", p. 11), is not explained beyond "complementary sources" (p. 3).
55	- Data availability (public? link?): [A] "We are working on a public release of the ProgramDistill benchmark" (p. 1). Not yet released at time of writing; prompts are given in the appendix (p. 25; p. 30; p. 33).
56	
57	## 5. Experimental setup
58	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Modified R2E-Gym harness with tools `execute_bash`, `file_editor`, `search` and `finish`. A browser CLI drives both the reference and the current app (p. 8). Agents see only structured text observations (visible text, element IDs, roles, accessible names, input values); full reconstruction additionally exposes selectors. Screenshots and raw HTML are excluded (p. 3; p. 24).
59	- [V] Partial reconstruction: reasoning effort high, at most 1,000 steps, 150k-token history cutoff. Full reconstruction: reasoning effort max, at most 10,000 steps, 500k-token cutoff. Per-tool timeout 90 s, no aggregate time limit (p. 24).
60	- [V] Determinism: application state is reset before each collection and replay, and a shared fake clock (libfaketime plus a browser Date offset) is used (p. 3; p. 19; p. 20).
61	- [V] Isolation: the reference is reachable only via the browser helper, public egress is blocked, there is no pre-mask git history, and grading traces are private. Submissions are rebuilt and replayed in a fresh verifier (p. 10; p. 23; p. 24).
62	- [V] The full-reconstruction scaffold requires an `app.js` exporting `async function handle(req, res, context)`, with state kept in `context.state` (p. 37).
63	- [V] Number of runs: one per model and task (partial) and one per model and app (36 full-reconstruction runs, p. 12). Repeats or seeds: not reported.
64	- [V] Cost: tokens x LiteLLM list prices (p. 37). One GPT-6 Astra pass over 300 tasks took about 557 minutes on 4 servers (p. 37).
65	- Code availability: [A] release in progress (p. 1).
66	
67	## 6. Evaluation metrics
68	- Replay verifier V(A, L): returns 1 only if every recorded browser action completes and every expected signal is satisfied, replaying the whole prerequisite lineage without LLM involvement (p. 4).
69	- Binary score: 1 only if the complete lineage passes after the agent's patch. Chain score: fraction of repair targets passed, giving partial credit (p. 6).
70	- Full reconstruction: atomic behaviour recovery (fraction of single-behaviour tests passed, with prerequisites replayed) and cumulative workflow recovery (binary and chain) (p. 6; p. 11).
71	- [V] Source-level matching is not required: function names, variables and structure may differ if behaviour replays (p. 6). [V] In full reconstruction, however, selectors and accessible names must match the reference, because evaluation "replays user interactions using selectors" (p. 35).
72	- Diagnostics: interaction counts (observation, read/search, edit/write steps), share of unchanged target files and retained stub lines, shortcut-attempt rate, failure categories (p. 9; p. 10; p. 12).
73	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [V] None; means only. Pearson correlations between prompt size and binary score are reported in the context-length check (p. 40).
74	
75	## 7. Key findings
76	1. [V] Partial reconstruction (ProgramDistill-300): mean binary score is 84.3% for GPT-6 Astra, 68.7% for Claude Opus 5 and 60.7% for GPT-5.6 Sol, with a middle tier at 45.3–48.3% and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview lowest at 22.3%. Mean cost per trajectory is $33.99, $28.86 and $16.01 for the top three (p. 8; p. 38).
77	2. [V] Success drops with restoration depth: Astra falls from 100% at depth 1 to 64.0% at depth 8, Opus 5 from 96% to 32.0% and Sol from 92% to 32.0%; every other model keeps less than half of its depth-1 performance (p. 8; p. 9).
78	3. [V] Restoring UI as well as logic is harder. Binary scores for logic-only vs logic-and-UI masks are 92.9% vs 76.9% for Astra and 76.4% vs 46.9% for Sol (p. 38).
79	4. [V] Full-application reconstruction (12 apps): Astra recovers 58.98% of atomic behaviours and 49.15% of cumulative workflows, Opus 5 42.03% and 28.81%, and Sol 33.39% and 21.07% (p. 11). Per-app results vary widely, e.g. Astra's cumulative recovery ranges from 81.8% (MailHub) to 5.9% (Baserow) (p. 11).
80	5. [V] Of 977 failed atomic behaviours in full reconstruction, 59.2% were never observed in the reference. Of the rest, 1.8% were observed but not implemented, 11.1% were implemented with the wrong observable form and 27.9% produced the wrong state, route or result (p. 12).
81	6. [A] Agents' own validation (syntax checks, successful requests, selected text matches) often did not recheck the failing workflow after the last relevant edit, so mismatches went undetected (p. 12; p. 13).
82	7. [V] From depth 1 to 8, code to restore grows 9.3x and required browser actions 10.7x, but reference-observation steps per target fall from 34.60 to 8.46. Retained mask stub lines rise from 11.1% to 24.6% (p. 9; p. 10).
83	8. [V] The depth effect persists among runs with similar context lengths; e.g. in the 40–80k band, mean binary score falls from 82.6% at depth 1 to 24.2% at depth 8 (p. 39).
84	9. [V] At least one shortcut attempt (git history, public source fetch, harness probing, direct reference access) appears in 7.2% of trajectories: 19.0% for Grok 4.6, 17.7% for Gemini 3.1 Pro and 0.3% for Astra. These channels were blocked by design (p. 10).
85	10. [V] The best model was the most observation-heavy and edit-light: Astra averages 96.3 current-app observation steps and 9.9 edit/write steps per trajectory (p. 9).
86	
87	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
88	- [A] Agents receive structured text observations, not screenshots. Visual fidelity is not evaluated and "would require criteria beyond the current replay-based behavioral checks" (p. 14).
89	- [A] Only self-contained web apps; external services, nondeterministic state, and desktop/mobile apps are future work (p. 14).
90	- [A] Benchmark coverage and quality depend on the construction model (GPT-5.6 Sol) (p. 15).
91	- [A] Results depend on the browser/agent infrastructure (replay-stable selectors, settled observations, harness), and sensitivity to these choices is uncharacterised (p. 15).
92	- [A] The isolation is not a general-purpose sandbox for hostile code (p. 24).
93	- [A] Possible misuse for cloning proprietary apps; experiments are limited to public/open-source apps (p. 15).
94	
95	## 9. Limitations we identified
96	- [I] Code quality and maintainability of the rebuilt or repaired code are not measured at all. Only behavioural replay is scored (p. 6). The full-reconstruction contract forces a single Node `handle()` entry with in-memory `context.state` (p. 37), while the originals use Django, Angular, React or Next.js with databases (p. 19). The rebuild's architecture is therefore imposed and not comparable to the original.
97	- [I] Possible self-preference and family bias:
98	  - GPT-5.6 Sol builds the traces, masks and problem statements (p. 2) and is also an evaluated model; the top model is from the same vendor (GPT-6 Astra) (p. 8).
99	  - The full-reconstruction failure analysis is done by GPT-6 Astra (p. 12), which judges its own and its competitors' failures, with no human validation reported.
100	- [I] No human check anywhere. Tasks are built "without human intervention" (p. 1), mask depth is judged by an LLM critic (p. 5), and 572 cumulative masks were merged by an LLM agent (p. 6). The only quality evidence is the replay checks and the 100% depth-1 solve rate of one model (p. 8). No sample of tasks was manually audited.
101	- [I] Oracle completeness is not measured. Unlike ProgramBench, no code coverage is reported for the trace suites. Behaviours exist only if the mining LLM found and stably replayed them; 29.5% of goals were lost (p. 7). Behaviours an agent never observes still count as failures (59.2% of failures, p. 12), but the trace bank itself may miss large parts of each app.
102	- [I] The full-reconstruction oracle checks surface identity (selectors, accessible names, labels) (p. 35), and the agent is shown the reference's selectors (p. 24). This mixes functional fidelity with DOM-level mimicry. A functionally equivalent rebuild with different labels would fail, while visual appearance is not checked at all (p. 14).
103	- [I] Contamination is not discussed. The 8 real-world apps are public GitHub projects (p. 19), so agents may partly reconstruct masked code from memory, especially for well-known clones.
104	- [I] Small and uneven samples for headline claims: one run per cell, full reconstruction on 12 apps x 3 models (36 runs) (p. 12), and per-app task pools from 2 to 372 (p. 19). Differences between close models (e.g. 45.3% vs 45.7%, p. 8) are not interpretable without variance estimates.
105	- [I] The model names (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol) were very recent at publication and are cited to system cards (p. 16; p. 17). Results may not be reproducible once these API versions change.
106	
107	## 10. Threats to validity
108	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [V] Leakage controls: no pre-mask git history, blocked egress, hidden grading files, browser-only reference access, fresh-verifier rebuild (p. 10; p. 24). [I] Remaining threats: the same model family builds and is evaluated; LLM-only task validation; memorisation of public source.
109	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] 26 mostly small, self-contained CRUD-style web apps, 18 of them from one synthetic suite (OSWorld) (p. 19); a single harness; text-only observation (p. 14). Transfer to large production apps, visual-design fidelity or human-in-the-loop vibe coding is untested.
110	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] Replay of mined traces is a sound behavioural oracle for the traced workflows, but it covers only discovered behaviours and also demands selector-level identity (p. 35). "Reconstruction success" therefore means reproducing specific recorded interactions, not the whole application.
111	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No CIs or tests; single runs; stratified 300-task subset. The depth trend is consistent across models and context bands (p. 39), which makes that particular finding more credible.
112	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Prompts, harness settings and pricing are reported in detail (p. 24; p. 25; p. 37). [A] The benchmark is not yet public (p. 1).
113	
114	## 11. Future research directions
115	- Stated by authors [A] (p. 14; p. 15):
116	  - add screenshots and visual-fidelity criteria;
117	  - extend to external services, nondeterministic state, and desktop and mobile apps;
118	  - study the quality–cost trade-off of the construction model;
119	  - characterise sensitivity to infrastructure choices;
120	  - use the tasks and trajectories for training (distillation, RL, curriculum by restoration depth).
121	- Suggested by us [I]:
122	  1. Measure code quality and maintainability of rebuilt apps, with a free architecture rather than a single fixed handler.
123	  2. Audit a sample of mined traces and masks by hand, and measure oracle coverage.
124	  3. Use a construction model from a different family than the evaluated models.
125	  4. Add repeated runs.
126	  5. Study a human-in-the-loop (vibe-coding) condition in which a developer steers reconstruction.
127	
128	## 12. Relevance to our research
129	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ4, RQ5 (RQ3 only as a documented gap).
130	- How it informs our work [I]: This is the closest available study of rebuilding *interactive web applications* from a running reference via its UI, which is our core scenario. It offers a reusable fidelity-testing method: deterministic replay of recorded browser workflows with expected signals and prerequisite lineages. It also gives a failure taxonomy showing that most misses come from not exploring the reference rather than from coding errors (p. 12). It shows that agents' self-validation is unreliable (p. 12). Together with ProgramBench (yang2026programbench), it shows that functional fidelity of whole-app rebuilds remains far from complete. Like ProgramBench, it does not measure the maintainability of the rebuilt code, which supports the joint fidelity-plus-quality gap in RQ5.
131	
132	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
133	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
134	|---|---|---|---|---|
135	| RQ1 | Reference-guided setting: agent interacts with a live reference web app via a browser CLI (structured text observations, no source, no screenshots) and edits a masked repo or a blank scaffold to reproduce its behaviour. | p. 3; p. 6; p. 24 | V | moderate (design fact) |
136	| RQ2 | Best full-application rebuild from a live reference recovers 58.98% of atomic behaviours and 49.15% of cumulative workflows (12 apps); other models 21–42%. | p. 11 | V | weak (preprint, 36 single runs) |
137	| RQ2 | Partial-repair success falls as more dependent behaviours must be restored (best model 100% at depth 1 to 64% at depth 8; others to ≤32%), and the drop persists when context length is controlled. | p. 8; p. 9; p. 39 | V | weak (single runs, but consistent across 9 models) |
138	| RQ2 | Restoring UI plus logic is harder than logic alone (e.g. 92.9% vs 76.9% binary for the best model). | p. 38 | V | weak |
139	| RQ2 | 59.2% of failed behaviours in full rebuilds were never observed in the reference; 27.9% had wrong state/result and 11.1% wrong observable form. | p. 12 | V | weak (classified by an LLM that is also an evaluated model) |
140	| RQ4 | Fidelity oracle: deterministic browser-trace replay with expected signals, admitted only if replayable on the intact app, failing after masking, and passing with the gold patch. | p. 4; p. 5; p. 6 | V | moderate (design fact) |
141	| RQ4 | Agents' own validation (syntax checks, request success, partial text checks) missed behavioural mismatches with the reference. | p. 12 | A | weak |
142	| RQ4 | Tasks are built and validated without human intervention by one LLM (GPT-5.6 Sol), which is also evaluated; authors note quality depends on the construction model. | p. 1; p. 2; p. 15 | A | weak |
143	| RQ5 | Visual fidelity and screenshot-based observation are not evaluated; authors name them, plus desktop/mobile apps, as future work. Code quality of rebuilds is not measured (our observation). | p. 14 | A | weak |
144	
145	## 14. Key quotes
146	> "The distinction is thus a shift from specification consumption to specification discovery." (p. 14)
147	
148	> "the largest failure category is behavior that was not observed in the reference, accounting for 59.2% of failures" (p. 12)
149	
150	> "Similar text or element structure in observations is not sufficient." (p. 35)
151	
152	## Analyst notes
153	- Reading coverage: whole paper read, pp. 1–40, including all appendices and prompts. Figures 1, 6, 8–13 are partly garbled in the text layer, so only numbers stated in the text or tables are used. Figure 11 per-model shortcut rates were cross-checked with the text (p. 10).
154	- Uncertainties:
155	  - how the 26 and 12 apps were chosen;
156	  - whether trace suites cover most app functionality;
157	  - how much memorisation of public app source contributes.
158	  
159	  The future-dated model names (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5, Gemini 3.7 Flash) are taken as reported; the paper is dated 16 Sep 2026, before our analysis date.
160	- Strength ratings follow research-standards §5 (preprint without replication = weak). The depth-degradation finding is the most robust internally, because it is consistent across 9 models and context bands.

discovered through interaction with fully functional reference applications. We build ProgramDistill by factorizing
                                             applications into features of different granularities, each associated with replayable behaviors executable via its
                                             gold patch. Our pipeline, mine-craft-patch, discovers 1,975 replay-verified behaviors across 26 applications
                                             and constructs 4,063 tasks without human intervention. Across nine frontier coding agents, GPT-6 Astra and
                                             Claude Opus 5 achieve 49.2% and 28.8% success on cumulative workflows in full-application reconstruction. In
                                             partial-application reconstruction, success falls from 100% to 64.0% and from 96% to 32% as restoration depth
                                             increases from 1 to 8. ProgramDistill thus provides a scalable benchmark with controlled difficulty for evaluating
                                             and diagnosing coding agents, and a natural basis for future curriculum-based training.

reveals a growing mismatch between reconstruction burden and agent effort, with observation effort per required

 - Use 'context.readBody()', 'context.json()', and 'context.html()' as needed.
 - The runtime hot-reloads repository modules on every request.
 - Faithfully implement the routes, labels, forms, selectors, state transitions,
   downloads, and validation behavior observed in the reference.

3	status: ready
4	evidence_basis: full-text
5	design: benchmark construction + comparative evaluation of 3 agent frameworks x LLMs; UI-agent (LLM) functional testing validated against 3 human testers; SFT training study
6	dataset: WebGen-Bench, 101 NL website-generation instructions with 647 GPT-4o-drafted, human-refined UI test cases; WebGen-Instruct 6,667 training instructions
7	sample_size: 101 instructions / 647 test cases x 16 framework-model settings (single run); human validation on 3 settings
8	metrics: accuracy = (YES + 0.5 PARTIAL)/total test cases judged by WebVoyager UI agent; appearance score 1-5 (GPT-4o); agent-human alignment rate
9	main_finding: Best general model setting (Bolt.diy + DeepSeek-R1) reaches 27.8% test-case accuracy on websites built from scratch; UI-agent judge agrees with humans on 86-94% of cases.
10	relevance: high
11	analysed: 2026-11-11
12	---
13	<!-- Frontmatter: single-line values; they feed literature-matrix.md via `rlab index`.
14	     status: draft (in progress) -> ready (analyst self-check passed) -> complete (critical review passed).
15	     evidence_basis: full-text | abstract-only. abstract-only analyses must not fill methodology detail.
16	     relevance: high | medium | low. -->
17	
18	# WebGen-Bench: Evaluating LLMs on Generating Interactive and Functional Websites from Scratch
19	
20	- Authors: Lu, Zimu; Yang, Yunqiao; Ren, Houxing; Hou, Haotian; Xiao, Han; Wang, Ke
21	- Year / venue: 2025, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (published)
22	- DOI: 10.52202/085713-2419 · URL: https://doi.org/10.52202/085713-2419
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
24	- Version note: the PDF we hold is arXiv v2 (11 Aug 2025), marked "Preprint. Under review." (p. 1), with the NeurIPS checklist appended (p. 37–43). Metadata records the NeurIPS 38 published version. Page refs refer to this arXiv PDF; the author line in the PDF (p. 1) lists Shi, Zhou, Zhan and Li and does not include "Hou, Haotian", who appears in `metadata.json` — the published author list may differ.
25	
26	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
27	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
28	
29	## 1. Research objective
30	[A] To measure how well LLM-based code agents can build complete, multi-file, interactive websites from scratch from natural-language instructions written for non-expert users, and to provide a training set that improves open models on this task (p. 1–3).
31	
32	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
33	No formal RQs or hypotheses. Stated contributions (p. 3):
34	- [A] A benchmark (WebGen-Bench) of website-generation instructions with test cases for functionality and appearance (p. 3).
35	- [A] An evaluation of three code-agent frameworks (Bolt.diy, OpenHands, Aider) with several LLMs (p. 3).
36	- [A] A training set (WebGen-Instruct, 6,667 instructions) and fine-tuned models (WebGen-LM 7B/14B/32B) (p. 3).
37	
38	## 3. Methodology
39	- Research design: benchmark construction; comparative evaluation of agent framework x LLM settings; validation of the automated judge against human testers; fine-tuning experiment with a training-size ablation (p. 4–10). [V]
40	- Approach / model / intervention: agents receive an instruction without technical details ("The agents should autonomously determine the optimal technical approach") and generate a website codebase from scratch (p. 5). [V]
41	- How functional correctness is tested: for each instruction GPT-4o drafted 5–10 atomic test cases (operation + expected result) covering every functional and appearance requirement; two CS PhD students independently reviewed and refined them and resolved discrepancies by discussion, giving 647 test cases (4–11 per instruction) (p. 5–6, p. 19). [V] Each test case is executed by the WebVoyager web-navigation agent driven by Qwen2.5-VL-32B-Instruct, which interacts with the site (at most 15 interactions), inspects screenshots and answers YES, PARTIAL or NO; if the limit is reached, a follow-up prompt forces a final decision (p. 6, p. 19–20). [V]
42	- How appearance is tested: GPT-4o grades screenshots 1–5 on rendering, content relevance, layout harmony and modernness (p. 6, p. 21). [V]
43	- Baselines or comparison conditions: three frameworks on DeepSeek-V3, Claude-3.5-Sonnet and DeepSeek-R1; then Bolt.diy with Claude-3.5-Sonnet, DeepSeek-R1, DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o, o3-mini, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, and the fine-tuned WebGen-LM models (p. 7–8). [V] No human-developer baseline. [V] (p. 7–8)
44	
45	## 4. Dataset and sample
46	- Data source(s): authors identified 20 web-application categories from freelance platforms (Upwork, Freelancer, Proginn); 40 CS PhD students brainstormed specific applications and requirements, producing 10,152 project descriptions; GPT-4o converted them into instructions with a one-shot prompt (p. 4–5, p. 15). [V]
47	- Sample size (N) and unit: test set 101 instructions; 647 test cases (p. 5–6). [V] Instruction categories: Content Presentation 28, User Interaction 49, Data Management 24 (p. 6, Table 2). [V] Test-case categories: Functional Testing 339, Data Display 186, Design Validation 122 — total 667 in Table 8 (p. 23), which does not match the 647 stated elsewhere (p. 1, p. 6). [V]
48	- Sampling / selection method: "two to eight representative examples from each category" sampled for the test set; how representativeness was judged is not reported (p. 5). [V] Training set decontaminated by 5-gram Jaccard (> 0.6 removed) and sentence-embedding cosine similarity (> 0.55 removed), plus manual inspection of top-3 matches (p. 5, p. 14). [V]
49	- Data availability (public? link?): data, code and model weights released under MIT licence at github.com/mnluzimu/WebGen-Bench (p. 1, p. 14). [A] (link not checked by us)
50	
51	## 5. Experimental setup
52	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: Bolt.diy (browser-based WebContainer; model picks frameworks such as Vite/React/Remix), OpenHands with CodeActAgent, Aider with adapted prompts; OpenHands told to use TypeScript/HTML/CSS with `npm install` / `npm run dev`; Aider told to prefer Vite and Node.js (p. 7, p. 21–22). [V] Models smaller than Qwen2.5-Coder-32B were excluded because they often failed the output format (p. 7). [V] Sampling temperature, number of runs and time/step budgets for generation: not reported.
53	- Training: 2K WebGen-Instruct instructions run through Bolt.diy with DeepSeek-V3; trajectories kept only if the GPT-4o appearance score ≥ 3 (600 trajectories); Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct 7B/14B/32B fine-tuned for 2 epochs, LR 4e-5, batch 32 (p. 7). [V]
54	- Code availability: released (p. 1, p. 14). [A]
55	- Evaluator-reliability design: three human testers independently annotated the full test results of Bolt.diy with Claude-3.5-Sonnet, DeepSeek-R1 and DeepSeek-V3; inconsistent cases went to a fourth tester for a final label; the agent's label was compared with this human label (alignment rate) (p. 8–9). [V] Appearance-score reliability: two extra model graders (o3, Claude-3.5-Sonnet) and manual grading of the same three settings (p. 22–23). [V] Number of human appearance graders: not reported.
56	
57	## 6. Evaluation metrics
58	- Accuracy — (N_YES + 0.5 × N_PARTIAL) / N_total × 100% over all test cases; websites that fail to start count as failures (p. 7–8, Table 3). [V]
59	- Yes / Partial / No / Start-failed rates (p. 8, Table 3). [V]
60	- Appearance score — GPT-4o grade 1–5 (p. 6). [V]
61	- Alignment rate — share of test cases where UI-agent label equals the human label (p. 9). [V] Inter-human agreement among the three testers: "we assessed the consistency of their annotations" (p. 8), but no value is reported. No chance-corrected statistic.
62	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): none; NeurIPS checklist answers "No" for error bars "because it would be too computationally expensive" (p. 40). [V]
63	
64	## 7. Key findings
65	1. Best general-model setting is Bolt.diy + DeepSeek-R1 at 27.8% accuracy (YES 24.7%), closely followed by Bolt.diy + Claude-3.5-Sonnet at 26.4% (p. 8, Table 3). [V]
66	2. Framework matters: with DeepSeek-V3, accuracy is 20.8% (Bolt.diy), 9.0% (OpenHands), 14.1% (Aider) (p. 8, Table 3). [V] Start-failure rates reach 38.6% (Bolt.diy + o3-mini) and 32.1% (Aider + Claude-3.5-Sonnet) (p. 8). [V]
67	3. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Coder-32B on 600 filtered trajectories raises accuracy from 9.5% to 38.2% (WebGen-LM-32B), above DeepSeek-R1 (p. 8, Table 3); accuracy rises with training size: 25.1% (150), 31.9% (300), 38.2% (600) (p. 10, Table 6). [V]
68	4. Functional test cases are hardest: e.g. Bolt.diy + DeepSeek-R1 scores 21.1% on Functional Testing vs 44.3% on Design Validation; Bolt.diy + Claude-3.5-Sonnet 17.1% vs 52.0% (p. 9, Table 4). [V] The authors conclude that "superficial aspects, such as color themes, are easier to implement than deeper internal functionalities" (p. 8). [A]
69	5. UI-agent vs human labels: alignment rate 90.3% (Claude-3.5-Sonnet), 86.1% (DeepSeek-R1), 94.4% (DeepSeek-V3); aggregate accuracy differs by 0.4–2.3 points (agent 26.4/27.8/20.8 vs manual 26.0/30.1/21.3) (p. 9, Table 5). [V]
70	6. Best appearance score 3.0 (Bolt.diy + Claude-3.5-Sonnet) (p. 8). [V] GPT-4o, o3, Claude-3.5-Sonnet and human graders give the same ranking of three settings, with GPT-4o scoring highest (p. 23, Table 9). [V]
71	7. Human manual testing of all 647 cases is estimated at ~10.8 hours and $377.8 per setting (60 s per case), the stated reason for automation (p. 6). [V]
72	
73	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
74	- [A] Websites are generated only with TypeScript, JavaScript, CSS and HTML; Python, Java, Go and other tools were not integrated (p. 14).
75	- [A] Only supervised fine-tuning was used; RL or DPO not explored (p. 14).
76	- [A] Training data was not scaled beyond 600 trajectories because of API budget (p. 9).
77	- [A] No error bars, for cost reasons (p. 40).
78	
79	## 9. Limitations we identified
80	- [I] The functional oracle is an LLM-driven UI agent with a 15-interaction cap (p. 19). Human validation covers only 3 of 16 settings, all Bolt.diy (p. 8–9); agreement may differ for OpenHands/Aider outputs or weaker models with many start failures. Alignment is reported as raw percent on a 3-class label without chance correction, and inter-human agreement is not reported (p. 8–9).
81	- [I] The alignment rate counts test cases; with 59–74% NO labels (p. 9, Table 5), a judge that says NO often gets high agreement by default. Per-class (YES vs NO) agreement is not given, so false-positive "YES" rates are unknown.
82	- [I] Test cases were drafted by GPT-4o from the same instruction the agent sees, and each checks one atomic requirement (p. 5, p. 19). They test whether a stated feature is visible and responds, not deeper behavioural correctness (data persistence, multi-step workflows, edge cases); "PARTIAL" earning half credit further softens the score (p. 7).
83	- [I] Count inconsistency: 647 test cases (p. 1, p. 6) vs 667 in Table 8 (p. 23); unexplained.
84	- [I] Single run per setting and no reported generation hyper-parameters (temperature, budgets) (p. 7–8, p. 40); differences of 1–2 points (e.g. 27.8 vs 26.4) are not separable from noise.
85	- [I] The models evaluated (Claude-3.5-Sonnet, GPT-4o, o3-mini, DeepSeek-V3/R1) are early-2025 models; absolute numbers are already dated relative to later benchmarks such as Vibe Code Bench (tran2026vibe) [I].
86	- [I] Fine-tuning trajectories were filtered by GPT-4o appearance score, not by functional tests (p. 7), yet gains are measured on functional accuracy; the training and test instructions share the same GPT-4o generation template and colour-requirement style (p. 15–18), so part of the gain may be format/style adaptation to the benchmark distribution despite n-gram/embedding decontamination.
87	- [I] No code-quality, security or maintainability measures are taken for the generated codebases.
88	- [I] Funding and conflicts: not reported in the main text.
89	
90	## 10. Threats to validity
91	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): framework prompts differ (OpenHands/Aider adapted prompts, p. 21–22), confounding framework comparisons with prompt design [I]. Decontamination of training vs test instructions is reported (p. 14) [V]. GPT-4o wrote instructions and test cases and is also an evaluated model (p. 5, p. 8) [V]; it scored low (12.8%), so no evident self-advantage [I].
92	- External (generalisability of sample/context): 101 synthetic instructions from student brainstorming, not real client requests (p. 4–5, p. 14) [V]; JS/TS web stack only (p. 14) [V]. Inputs are NL instructions, not screenshots or existing apps [I].
93	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): atomic UI-agent tests capture visible feature presence and simple interactions; appearance score mixes rendering correctness with aesthetics (p. 21) [V/I]. No measure of code quality [I].
94	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): no error bars or tests (p. 40) [V]; three-setting human validation [V].
95	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): prompts for instruction generation, test generation, UI-agent testing, appearance grading and agents printed (p. 15–22) [V]; code, data and weights released (p. 1) [A]; generation sampling settings not reported.
96	
97	## 11. Future research directions
98	- Stated by authors [A]: support more languages and tools for website generation; explore RL and DPO post-training (p. 14); add more training data or data augmentation (p. 9).
99	- Suggested by us [I]: report per-class judge agreement and inter-human agreement; validate the judge on all frameworks; extend test cases from atomic checks to multi-step workflows (as Vibe Code Bench does); add code-quality metrics; for reconstruction, generate test cases from an existing site's observed behaviour rather than from an instruction.
100	
101	## 12. Relevance to our research
102	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (agent frameworks generating whole websites from NL instructions — Bolt.diy, OpenHands, Aider), RQ2 (functional fidelity via UI-agent test cases; headline accuracy), RQ4 (LLM-judge vs human alignment, test-case construction, no error bars), RQ5 (code quality not measured).
103	- How it informs our work [I]: WebGen-Bench established the pattern now common in this area: LLM-drafted, human-refined requirement-level test cases executed by a vision UI agent, with a human-alignment check. Its numbers show that visual/design requirements are met far more often than functional ones (p. 9), which matters for UI-based reconstruction: a rebuild can look right while behaving wrongly. The judge validation (86–94% alignment on 3 settings) is the main evidence that UI-agent testing is usable, but it is limited in scope and statistics.
104	
105	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
106	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
107	|---|---|---|---|---|
108	| RQ2 | Best general-LLM agent setting (Bolt.diy + DeepSeek-R1) reaches only 27.8% accuracy on 647 UI test cases for 101 websites built from scratch | 8 | V | moderate |
109	| RQ2 | Functional test cases are passed far less often than design-validation ones (e.g. 21.1% vs 44.3% for Bolt.diy + DeepSeek-R1; 17.1% vs 52.0% for Claude-3.5-Sonnet) | 9 | V | moderate |
110	| RQ1 | Agent framework strongly affects outcome: DeepSeek-V3 scores 20.8% in Bolt.diy, 14.1% in Aider, 9.0% in OpenHands | 8 | V | weak |
111	| RQ1 | Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Coder-32B on 600 filtered agent trajectories lifts accuracy from 9.5% to 38.2% | 8 | V | weak |
112	| RQ4 | Functional fidelity is judged by a WebVoyager UI agent (Qwen2.5-VL-32B) on GPT-4o-drafted, human-refined atomic test cases, with YES/PARTIAL/NO and half credit for PARTIAL | 6 | V | moderate |
113	| RQ4 | UI-agent labels match adjudicated human labels on 86.1–94.4% of test cases (3 Bolt.diy settings); inter-human agreement and chance-corrected agreement not reported | 9 | V | moderate |
114	| RQ4 | No error bars or significance tests; single run per setting | 40 | V | strong |
115	| RQ4 | GPT-4o appearance scores give the same ranking as o3, Claude-3.5-Sonnet and human grading on 3 settings | 23 | V | weak |
116	| RQ4 | Test-case total inconsistent (647 in text vs 667 in Table 8), illustrating weak reporting of benchmark composition | 23 | V | weak |
117	
118	## 14. Key quotes
119	> "The best-performing combination, Bolt.diy powered by DeepSeek-R1, achieves only 27.8% accuracy on the test cases" (p. 1)
120	> "This indicates that superficial aspects, such as color themes, are easier to implement than deeper internal functionalities." (p. 8)
121	> "Error bars are not reported because it would be too computationally expensive." (p. 40)
122	
123	## Analyst notes
124	- Reading coverage: main text p. 1–10, references p. 11–13, appendices A–N p. 14–25 read; UI-agent trajectory examples (p. 26–36) skimmed; NeurIPS checklist (p. 37–43) checked for statistics and human-subject answers. Figures 2, 3, 14–16 are images; only text values used. Section 3.1 paragraph "Web Development Project Descriptions Collection" appears twice on p. 5 (duplicated in the PDF).
125	- Uncertainties: the published NeurIPS version may differ from this arXiv v2 (e.g. the appendix says "We will add this discussion to the revised paper", p. 23). Author list mismatch with metadata (see version note). 647 vs 667 test-case count. Number of human appearance graders not reported.
126

8	metrics: accuracy = (YES + 0.5 PARTIAL)/total test cases judged by WebVoyager UI agent; appearance score 1-5 (GPT-4o); agent-human alignment rate
9	main_finding: Best general model setting (Bolt.diy + DeepSeek-R1) reaches 27.8% test-case accuracy on websites built from scratch; UI-agent judge agrees with humans on 86-94% of cases.

13	<!-- Frontmatter: single-line values; they feed literature-matrix.md via `rlab index`.
14	     status: draft (in progress) -> ready (analyst self-check passed) -> complete (critical review passed).
15	     evidence_basis: full-text | abstract-only. abstract-only analyses must not fill methodology detail.
16	     relevance: high | medium | low. -->
17	
18	# WebGen-Bench: Evaluating LLMs on Generating Interactive and Functional Websites from Scratch
19	
20	- Authors: Lu, Zimu; Yang, Yunqiao; Ren, Houxing; Hou, Haotian; Xiao, Han; Wang, Ke
21	- Year / venue: 2025, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (published)
22	- DOI: 10.52202/085713-2419 · URL: https://doi.org/10.52202/085713-2419
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
24	- Version note: the PDF we hold is arXiv v2 (11 Aug 2025), marked "Preprint. Under review." (p. 1), with the NeurIPS checklist appended (p. 37–43). Metadata records the NeurIPS 38 published version. Page refs refer to this arXiv PDF; the author line in the PDF (p. 1) lists Shi, Zhou, Zhan and Li and does not include "Hou, Haotian", who appears in `metadata.json` — the published author list may differ.
25	
26	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
27	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
28	
29	## 1. Research objective
30	[A] To measure how well LLM-based code agents can build complete, multi-file, interactive websites from scratch from natural-language instructions written for non-expert users, and to provide a training set that improves open models on this task (p. 1–3).
31	
32	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
33	No formal RQs or hypotheses. Stated contributions (p. 3):
34	- [A] A benchmark (WebGen-Bench) of website-generation instructions with test cases for functionality and appearance (p. 3).
35	- [A] An evaluation of three code-agent frameworks (Bolt.diy, OpenHands, Aider) with several LLMs (p. 3).
36	- [A] A training set (WebGen-Instruct, 6,667 instructions) and fine-tuned models (WebGen-LM 7B/14B/32B) (p. 3).
37	
38	## 3. Methodology
39	- Research design: benchmark construction; comparative evaluation of agent framework x LLM settings; validation of the automated judge against human testers; fine-tuning experiment with a training-size ablation (p. 4–10). [V]
40	- Approach / model / intervention: agents receive an instruction without technical details ("The agents should autonomously determine the optimal technical approach") and generate a website codebase from scratch (p. 5). [V]
41	- How functional correctness is tested: for each instruction GPT-4o drafted 5–10 atomic test cases (operation + expected result) covering every functional and appearance requirement; two CS PhD students independently reviewed and refined them and resolved discrepancies by discussion, giving 647 test cases (4–11 per instruction) (p. 5–6, p. 19). [V] Each test case is executed by the WebVoyager web-navigation agent driven by Qwen2.5-VL-32B-Instruct, which interacts with the site (at most 15 interactions), inspects screenshots and answers YES, PARTIAL or NO; if the limit is reached, a follow-up prompt forces a final decision (p. 6, p. 19–20). [V]
42	- How appearance is tested: GPT-4o grades screenshots 1–5 on rendering, content relevance, layout harmony and modernness (p. 6, p. 21). [V]
43	- Baselines or comparison conditions: three frameworks on DeepSeek-V3, Claude-3.5-Sonnet and DeepSeek-R1; then Bolt.diy with Claude-3.5-Sonnet, DeepSeek-R1, DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o, o3-mini, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, and the fine-tuned WebGen-LM models (p. 7–8). [V] No human-developer baseline. [V] (p. 7–8)
44	
45	## 4. Dataset and sample
46	- Data source(s): authors identified 20 web-application categories from freelance platforms (Upwork, Freelancer, Proginn); 40 CS PhD students brainstormed specific applications and requirements, producing 10,152 project descriptions; GPT-4o converted them into instructions with a one-shot prompt (p. 4–5, p. 15). [V]
47	- Sample size (N) and unit: test set 101 instructions; 647 test cases (p. 5–6). [V] Instruction categories: Content Presentation 28, User Interaction 49, Data Management 24 (p. 6, Table 2). [V] Test-case categories: Functional Testing 339, Data Display 186, Design Validation 122 — total 667 in Table 8 (p. 23), which does not match the 647 stated elsewhere (p. 1, p. 6). [V]
48	- Sampling / selection method: "two to eight representative examples from each category" sampled for the test set; how representativeness was judged is not reported (p. 5). [V] Training set decontaminated by 5-gram Jaccard (> 0.6 removed) and sentence-embedding cosine similarity (> 0.55 removed), plus manual inspection of top-3 matches (p. 5, p. 14). [V]
49	- Data availability (public? link?): data, code and model weights released under MIT licence at github.com/mnluzimu/WebGen-Bench (p. 1, p. 14). [A] (link not checked by us)
50	
51	## 5. Experimental setup
52	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: Bolt.diy (browser-based WebContainer; model picks frameworks such as Vite/React/Remix), OpenHands with CodeActAgent, Aider with adapted prompts; OpenHands told to use TypeScript/HTML/CSS with `npm install` / `npm run dev`; Aider told to prefer Vite and Node.js (p. 7, p. 21–22). [V] Models smaller than Qwen2.5-Coder-32B were excluded because they often failed the output format (p. 7). [V] Sampling temperature, number of runs and time/step budgets for generation: not reported.
53	- Training: 2K WebGen-Instruct instructions run through Bolt.diy with DeepSeek-V3; trajectories kept only if the GPT-4o appearance score ≥ 3 (600 trajectories); Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct 7B/14B/32B fine-tuned for 2 epochs, LR 4e-5, batch 32 (p. 7). [V]
54	- Code availability: released (p. 1, p. 14). [A]
55	- Evaluator-reliability design: three human testers independently annotated the full test results of Bolt.diy with Claude-3.5-Sonnet, DeepSeek-R1 and DeepSeek-V3; inconsistent cases went to a fourth tester for a final label; the agent's label was compared with this human label (alignment rate) (p. 8–9). [V] Appearance-score reliability: two extra model graders (o3, Claude-3.5-Sonnet) and manual grading of the same three settings (p. 22–23). [V] Number of human appearance graders: not reported.
56	
57	## 6. Evaluation metrics
58	- Accuracy — (N_YES + 0.5 × N_PARTIAL) / N_total × 100% over all test cases; websites that fail to start count as failures (p. 7–8, Table 3). [V]
59	- Yes / Partial / No / Start-failed rates (p. 8, Table 3). [V]
60	- Appearance score — GPT-4o grade 1–5 (p. 6). [V]
61	- Alignment rate — share of test cases where UI-agent label equals the human label (p. 9). [V] Inter-human agreement among the three testers: "we assessed the consistency of their annotations" (p. 8), but no value is reported. No chance-corrected statistic.
62	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): none; NeurIPS checklist answers "No" for error bars "because it would be too computationally expensive" (p. 40). [V]
63	
64	## 7. Key findings
65	1. Best general-model setting is Bolt.diy + DeepSeek-R1 at 27.8% accuracy (YES 24.7%), closely followed by Bolt.diy + Claude-3.5-Sonnet at 26.4% (p. 8, Table 3). [V]
66	2. Framework matters: with DeepSeek-V3, accuracy is 20.8% (Bolt.diy), 9.0% (OpenHands), 14.1% (Aider) (p. 8, Table 3). [V] Start-failure rates reach 38.6% (Bolt.diy + o3-mini) and 32.1% (Aider + Claude-3.5-Sonnet) (p. 8). [V]
67	3. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Coder-32B on 600 filtered trajectories raises accuracy from 9.5% to 38.2% (WebGen-LM-32B), above DeepSeek-R1 (p. 8, Table 3); accuracy rises with training size: 25.1% (150), 31.9% (300), 38.2% (600) (p. 10, Table 6). [V]
68	4. Functional test cases are hardest: e.g. Bolt.diy + DeepSeek-R1 scores 21.1% on Functional Testing vs 44.3% on Design Validation; Bolt.diy + Claude-3.5-Sonnet 17.1% vs 52.0% (p. 9, Table 4). [V] The authors conclude that "superficial aspects, such as color themes, are easier to implement than deeper internal functionalities" (p. 8). [A]
69	5. UI-agent vs human labels: alignment rate 90.3% (Claude-3.5-Sonnet), 86.1% (DeepSeek-R1), 94.4% (DeepSeek-V3); aggregate accuracy differs by 0.4–2.3 points (agent 26.4/27.8/20.8 vs manual 26.0/30.1/21.3) (p. 9, Table 5). [V]
70	6. Best appearance score 3.0 (Bolt.diy + Claude-3.5-Sonnet) (p. 8). [V] GPT-4o, o3, Claude-3.5-Sonnet and human graders give the same ranking of three settings, with GPT-4o scoring highest (p. 23, Table 9). [V]
71	7. Human manual testing of all 647 cases is estimated at ~10.8 hours and $377.8 per setting (60 s per case), the stated reason for automation (p. 6). [V]
72	
73	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
74	- [A] Websites are generated only with TypeScript, JavaScript, CSS and HTML; Python, Java, Go and other tools were not integrated (p. 14).
75	- [A] Only supervised fine-tuning was used; RL or DPO not explored (p. 14).
76	- [A] Training data was not scaled beyond 600 trajectories because of API budget (p. 9).
77	- [A] No error bars, for cost reasons (p. 40).
78	
79	## 9. Limitations we identified
80	- [I] The functional oracle is an LLM-driven UI agent with a 15-interaction cap (p. 19). Human validation covers only 3 of 16 settings, all Bolt.diy (p. 8–9); agreement may differ for OpenHands/Aider outputs or weaker models with many start failures. Alignment is reported as raw percent on a 3-class label without chance correction, and inter-human agreement is not reported (p. 8–9).
81	- [I] The alignment rate counts test cases; with 59–74% NO labels (p. 9, Table 5), a judge that says NO often gets high agreement by default. Per-class (YES vs NO) agreement is not given, so false-positive "YES" rates are unknown.
82	- [I] Test cases were drafted by GPT-4o from the same instruction the agent sees, and each checks one atomic requirement (p. 5, p. 19). They test whether a stated feature is visible and responds, not deeper behavioural correctness (data persistence, multi-step workflows, edge cases); "PARTIAL" earning half credit further softens the score (p. 7).
83	- [I] Count inconsistency: 647 test cases (p. 1, p. 6) vs 667 in Table 8 (p. 23); unexplained.
84	- [I] Single run per setting and no reported generation hyper-parameters (temperature, budgets) (p. 7–8, p. 40); differences of 1–2 points (e.g. 27.8 vs 26.4) are not separable from noise.
85	- [I] The models evaluated (Claude-3.5-Sonnet, GPT-4o, o3-mini, DeepSeek-V3/R1) are early-2025 models; absolute numbers are already dated relative to later benchmarks such as Vibe Code Bench (tran2026vibe) [I].
86	- [I] Fine-tuning trajectories were filtered by GPT-4o appearance score, not by functional tests (p. 7), yet gains are measured on functional accuracy; the training and test instructions share the same GPT-4o generation template and colour-requirement style (p. 15–18), so part of the gain may be format/style adaptation to the benchmark distribution despite n-gram/embedding decontamination.
87	- [I] No code-quality, security or maintainability measures are taken for the generated codebases.
88	- [I] Funding and conflicts: not reported in the main text.
89	
90	## 10. Threats to validity
91	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): framework prompts differ (OpenHands/Aider adapted prompts, p. 21–22), confounding framework comparisons with prompt design [I]. Decontamination of training vs test instructions is reported (p. 14) [V]. GPT-4o wrote instructions and test cases and is also an evaluated model (p. 5, p. 8) [V]; it scored low (12.8%), so no evident self-advantage [I].
92	- External (generalisability of sample/context): 101 synthetic instructions from student brainstorming, not real client requests (p. 4–5, p. 14) [V]; JS/TS web stack only (p. 14) [V]. Inputs are NL instructions, not screenshots or existing apps [I].
93	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): atomic UI-agent tests capture visible feature presence and simple interactions; appearance score mixes rendering correctness with aesthetics (p. 21) [V/I]. No measure of code quality [I].
94	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): no error bars or tests (p. 40) [V]; three-setting human validation [V].
95	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): prompts for instruction generation, test generation, UI-agent testing, appearance grading and agents printed (p. 15–22) [V]; code, data and weights released (p. 1) [A]; generation sampling settings not reported.
96	
97	## 11. Future research directions
98	- Stated by authors [A]: support more languages and tools for website generation; explore RL and DPO post-training (p. 14); add more training data or data augmentation (p. 9).
99	- Suggested by us [I]: report per-class judge agreement and inter-human agreement; validate the judge on all frameworks; extend test cases from atomic checks to multi-step workflows (as Vibe Code Bench does); add code-quality metrics; for reconstruction, generate test cases from an existing site's observed behaviour rather than from an instruction.
100	
101	## 12. Relevance to our research
102	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (agent frameworks generating whole websites from NL instructions — Bolt.diy, OpenHands, Aider), RQ2 (functional fidelity via UI-agent test cases; headline accuracy), RQ4 (LLM-judge vs human alignment, test-case construction, no error bars), RQ5 (code quality not measured).
103	- How it informs our work [I]: WebGen-Bench established the pattern now common in this area: LLM-drafted, human-refined requirement-level test cases executed by a vision UI agent, with a human-alignment check. Its numbers show that visual/design requirements are met far more often than functional ones (p. 9), which matters for UI-based reconstruction: a rebuild can look right while behaving wrongly. The judge validation (86–94% alignment on 3 settings) is the main evidence that UI-agent testing is usable, but it is limited in scope and statistics.
104	
105	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
106	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
107	|---|---|---|---|---|
108	| RQ2 | Best general-LLM agent setting (Bolt.diy + DeepSeek-R1) reaches only 27.8% accuracy on 647 UI test cases for 101 websites built from scratch | 8 | V | moderate |
109	| RQ2 | Functional test cases are passed far less often than design-validation ones (e.g. 21.1% vs 44.3% for Bolt.diy + DeepSeek-R1; 17.1% vs 52.0% for Claude-3.5-Sonnet) | 9 | V | moderate |
110	| RQ1 | Agent framework strongly affects outcome: DeepSeek-V3 scores 20.8% in Bolt.diy, 14.1% in Aider, 9.0% in OpenHands | 8 | V | weak |
111	| RQ1 | Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Coder-32B on 600 filtered agent trajectories lifts accuracy from 9.5% to 38.2% | 8 | V | weak |
112	| RQ4 | Functional fidelity is judged by a WebVoyager UI agent (Qwen2.5-VL-32B) on GPT-4o-drafted, human-refined atomic test cases, with YES/PARTIAL/NO and half credit for PARTIAL | 6 | V | moderate |
113	| RQ4 | UI-agent labels match adjudicated human labels on 86.1–94.4% of test cases (3 Bolt.diy settings); inter-human agreement and chance-corrected agreement not reported | 9 | V | moderate |
114	| RQ4 | No error bars or significance tests; single run per setting | 40 | V | strong |
115	| RQ4 | GPT-4o appearance scores give the same ranking as o3, Claude-3.5-Sonnet and human grading on 3 settings | 23 | V | weak |
116	| RQ4 | Test-case total inconsistent (647 in text vs 667 in Table 8), illustrating weak reporting of benchmark composition | 23 | V | weak |
117	
118	## 14. Key quotes
119	> "The best-performing combination, Bolt.diy powered by DeepSeek-R1, achieves only 27.8% accuracy on the test cases" (p. 1)
120	> "This indicates that superficial aspects, such as color themes, are easier to implement than deeper internal functionalities." (p. 8)
121	> "Error bars are not reported because it would be too computationally expensive." (p. 40)
122	
123	## Analyst notes
124	- Reading coverage: main text p. 1–10, references p. 11–13, appendices A–N p. 14–25 read; UI-agent trajectory examples (p. 26–36) skimmed; NeurIPS checklist (p. 37–43) checked for statistics and human-subject answers. Figures 2, 3, 14–16 are images; only text values used. Section 3.1 paragraph "Web Development Project Descriptions Collection" appears twice on p. 5 (duplicated in the PDF).
125	- Uncertainties: the published NeurIPS version may differ from this arXiv v2 (e.g. the appendix says "We will add this discussion to the revised paper", p. 23). Author list mismatch with metadata (see version note). 647 vs 667 test-case count. Number of human appearance graders not reported.
