## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [V] RQ1: How does the quality of production code vary across interaction models? Sub-questions: RQ1.1 syntactic similarity, RQ1.2 functional correctness, RQ1.3 complexity (p. 11, p. 12).
- [V] RQ2: How does the quality of the tests vary? RQ2.1 structural complexity of tests, RQ2.2 coverage (p. 13).
- [V] RQ3: How does TDD process efficiency vary? (p. 13)
- [V] Statistical null hypotheses per pairwise comparison are one-tailed (H0: A <= B, per Tables 9-13) (p. 25, p. 27); no substantive directional hypotheses stated up front.

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] Model confound: collaborative and fully-automated workflows used GPT-3.5 Turbo (p. 14, p. 17), while agentic runs used ChatGPT 5 and Claude Sonnet 4 (p. 17). The agentic advantage in TPR and time cannot be separated from the large model-generation gap. The authors call ChatGPT 5 "the most similar" model (p. 17), which we find hard to accept. This undermines the cross-workflow comparison that drives the main conclusions.
- [I] Very small groups: 9 vs 7 humans (p. 16), 3 fully-automated runs (p. 42). Repeated runs of the same configuration are not independent participants, yet they enter the same Mann-Whitney tests as people. With n = 3 (fully-automated) the minimum attainable one-tailed p-value is limited, so non-significance there is uninformative.
- [I] Design inconsistency: a Static-Group Comparison is, by definition, a design without randomisation, yet participants are said to be "randomly assigned" (p. 14, p. 15); 5 of the 16 came from an earlier preliminary session (p. 13), so session is a possible confound. No pre-test of skill; groups differ in experience (Table 5, p. 16).
- [I] Time is self-reported by humans (rounded to minutes, values like 2,400 s) but machine-measured for automated runs (p. 13, p. 41). Differences in Time mix measurement methods.
- [I] Two tiny string-formatting tasks with a 12-assertion oracle (p. 12) say little about application-level generation. TPR is assertion-level (e.g. 8.3% = 1/12).
- [I] The paper's "vibe coding" condition forbids prompt modification (p. 15) and uses scripted prompts, so it does not represent free-form vibe coding. Conclusions about "vibe coding" should be read as conclusions about this structured TDD workflow.
- [I] Some claims go beyond the data: the claim that humans "can reach the same level of correctness in collaborative settings" (p. 26) rests on single participants (P13: 100%) while the collaborative mean is 60.8% (p. 41). The Related Work states "the agentic workflow statistically produces higher-quality code" (p. 40), which conflicts with the higher complexity and lower coverage reported (p. 27, p. 35).
- [I] MCC is the only maintainability proxy; no code smells, readability or static-analysis measures.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Model generation confounded with workflow (see section 9); session (preliminary vs main) and experience imbalance; self-reported vs measured time. [A] Possible hidden AI use (p. 15).
- External (generalisability of sample/context): [A] Simple tasks, single CLLM for human workflows (p. 37). [I] Python-only, function-level tasks, one agentic platform; results do not transfer to multi-file applications or UI work.
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] TPR against a 12-assertion spec-derived suite is a reasonable small-scale functional-correctness oracle; MCC alone is a thin proxy for maintainability; lower baseline coverage of agentic code partly reflects added validation/logging rather than lower quality.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [V] Holm-Bonferroni correction and effect sizes reported (p. 10, p. 11). [A] Low power acknowledged (p. 36). [I] Non-independent repeated runs pooled as samples; no confidence intervals; one-tailed tests chosen for every direction.
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Prompts (Table 7, p. 20), metrics definitions (p. 14), per-participant data (p. 41, p. 42) and GitHub package (p. 43). [I] Agentic runs via a web interface of a commercial platform are hard to reproduce; model parameters not reported.

I applied every review fix for the five keys after checking each one against the cited page in `fulltext.txt`. I rejected none; for liu fix 2 I used a corrected range. cite-check passes, all five stay `status: ready`, and each now names the PDF version it was analysed from.

**liu2026benchmarking** (the priority fix)
- **Fix 1, the "~12x" [V] claim: applied.** I checked Table 3 (p. 6). The paper states no cost ratio anywhere. The new §7 finding 3, §13 RQ1 row and `main_finding` say:
  - MapCoder, ChatDev and MetaGPT cost several times more than Vanilla, but the amounts are small.
  - GPT-4o ChatDev: $0.1947 vs $0.0160, about 12x. Claude-Haiku ChatDev: $0.174 vs $0.015, about 11.6x.
  - Qwen-7B: ChatDev about 25x and MetaGPT about 69x. Vanilla's $0.0003 is rounded to 4 decimals, so these two ratios are imprecise.
  - Self-Collaboration, which the paper counts as multi-agent (p. 5), costs about the same as Vanilla.
  - The ratios are labelled [I] as our own arithmetic.
  - I also checked the "take longer" part: all four multi-agent frameworks are slower than Vanilla on every backbone (p. 6).
- **Fix 2, Table 10 vs Table 3: applied, with a different range.** The reviewer's "0.2–0.5 points" is too narrow. The gaps run from 0 (e.g. Qwen-7B GPT-Engineer 0.2403 vs 24.03) to about 7 points (Qwen-7B ChatDev 0.1803 vs 10.96, p. 25 vs p. 6). I added this to §9 and a cross-reference in §7 finding 2.
- **Version:** published ACL Anthology PDF, not arXiv 2510.14509.
- **Not fixed (outside the review list):** `main_finding` still says multi-agent frameworks "rarely beat" plain Vanilla. By my count from Table 3, 9 of 24 multi-agent cells beat Vanilla on Req.Acc, mostly by small margins. The paper's own wording is "do not consistently improve" (p. 6). This needs a decision before the analysis is marked complete.

**kim2026programdistill**: all 3 applied.
- Fix 1: full reconstruction is [V] 36 runs = 12 apps x 3 models (p. 11–12). For partial reconstruction, runs per task are not stated; "presumably one" is now [I]. `sample_size` now says "runs per task not stated".
- Fix 2: new §9 [I] bullet. The "Across nine frontier coding agents" wording (p. 1, repeated on p. 2) covers full reconstruction, but only 3 models were run there (p. 11).
- Fix 3: "in-memory" is replaced by the verbatim "so the verifier can reset it" (p. 37).
- Version: arXiv v1, 16 Sep 2026 (p. 1).

**lu2025webgen**: 2 applied, 1 not mine to apply.
- Fix 1: Table 8's categories 339 + 186 + 122 = 647 (p. 23), so "Total 667" is a typo. I corrected §4, §9 and the Analyst notes, and deleted the RQ4 evidence row.
- Fix 2: NO rates are 58.1–73.9 (p. 9), so the text now says "58–74%".
- Fix 3 (author list in `metadata.json`) is for you: it needs re-resolution via `rlab`. The analysis already flags it, and I did not touch metadata.
- Version: arXiv v2, 11 Aug 2025, pre-acceptance (p. 1).

**mock2026vibe**: 1 applied.
- I confirmed the test-direction problem in Table 9 (p. 25) and Table 10 (p. 27). It affects some rows, not all: "fully-automated > solo" has δ −0.15 and p = 0.685, which is as expected, and I note this.
- Added a §9 bullet, a §2 note and a §10 pointer.
- Version: published Springer open-access version of record (2027) 32:40.

**molison2025llm**: 2 applied.
- Fix 1: the §13 row now reads "OR 0.00–0.019, all p<0.001; the 0.00 implies a zero cell" (Table II, p. 8).
- Fix 2: I reworded the "≤ 0.19%" point using the paper's own way of writing odds ratios as percentages ("0.05% of the odds", p. 6).
- Version: arXiv v1, 1 Aug 2025 (p. 1).

**cite-check:** the command needs file arguments, so I passed the five analyses. Result: kim 90, liu 88, lu 78, mock 95, molison 97 citations; "cite-check: OK".

**Not done:** I did not run `rlab index`, because it rewrites files you told me not to touch. Run it so that the edited `main_finding` (liu) and `sample_size` (kim) reach the literature matrix.
